t.1.86.2: Yayāti said: The student who studies when summoned, who needs no prodding in his teacher's tasks, who rises before him and lies down to sleep after him, who is gentle, self-controlled, steadfast and heedful, and devoted to the recitation of the Veda, attains success.
t.1.86.1: How does the householder, living rightly, go to the gods? How the mendicant, how the one who performs his teacher's work, and how the forest-dweller settled on the good path? On this matter they now declare many things.
t.1.86.3: Having obtained wealth that has come by dharma, one should offer sacrifice, give gifts, and always feed guests, never taking what others have not given; this is the ancient secret teaching for the householder.
t.1.86.4: Living by his own strength, turned away from wrongdoing, a giver to others and never one who torments others, restrained in his food and his actions while dwelling in the forest, such a sage attains the highest perfection.
t.1.86.5: He who does not live by a craft, who is ever without a house, who has conquered his senses and is freed on every side, who goes about homeless, light, and moving little, wandering through the lands alone, he is a bhikṣu.
t.1.86.7: The forest-dweller who casts off the elements of his own body in the forest places ten kinsmen before him and ten after, together with himself as the twenty-first, in the realm of good deeds.
t.1.86.8: Aṣṭaka said: How many kinds of munis are there, and how many kinds of silence? Tell us that, for we wish to hear it.
t.1.86.6: The night by which the worlds are won and become blissful, and desires are conquered, on that very night the wise man, with his self restrained, should strive to become a dweller in the forest.
t.1.86.10: Aṣṭaka said: How, pray, is the village left behind for one who dwells in the forest? And for one who dwells in the village, how is the forest left behind?
t.1.86.9: He who, while dwelling in the forest, has the village behind him, or who, while dwelling in the village, has the forest behind him, would be a muni, O lord of men.
t.1.86.11: He who would be a forest-dwelling sage should not make use of what belongs to the village; thus, as he dwells in the forest, the village is left behind him.
t.1.86.12: The sage should be without a sacred fire and without a home, belonging to no clan or Vedic school, and he should desire only so much clothing as will cover his loins.
t.1.86.14: But the sage who, having renounced desires, has abandoned action and conquered his senses, and who abides in silence, would attain perfection in the world.
t.1.86.13: He should desire only as much food as is needed to keep life going; in this way, even while he dwells in a village, the forest stands at his back.
t.1.86.16: When the sage, emaciated and worn thin by austerity, his flesh, bones and blood wasted away, becomes free from the pairs of opposites and has taken up the vow of silence, then, having conquered this world, he wins the world beyond.
t.1.86.15: With teeth cleansed and nails pared, always bathed and adorned, dark himself yet abiding in bright deeds, who would not be fit to honor such a man?
t.1.86.17: But when the sage seeks his food with his mouth alone, like a cow, then that world which was earlier his becomes fit for immortality.
